title: Do I Really Need Insurance for My Cleaning Business?
excerpt: Many new cleaners ask whether insurance is a legal requirement. Here is what the law says, and why going without is a big risk.
metaTitle: Do I Need Cleaning Insurance? UK Guide
metaDescription: Do you need insurance for your cleaning business? What UK law says about employers' liability, why public liability matters and the risks of going without.
keywords: is cleaning insurance a legal requirement
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: A cleaner inspecting a cream carpet in a bright living room
content:
Starting a cleaning business is an exciting venture. You have your equipment, your first few clients, and you are ready to make spaces sparkle. But one question nags at many new business owners: do I actually need insurance?

The short answer

For most sole traders, public liability insurance is not a legal requirement in the UK. Employers' liability insurance is different: it is compulsory for most businesses as soon as they employ anyone. You can read more about that in our guide to employers' liability insurance for cleaning companies.

Operating without public liability cover is still widely considered a serious gamble. Many commercial clients and letting agents will not use a cleaner who cannot show a certificate, and a single claim could cost far more than a year's premiums.

Why take the risk?

Cleaning is physical work involving chemicals, water and other people's property. Over time, accidents are likely to happen, however careful you are:

  • Bleach spilt on a client's expensive wool carpet.
  • A visitor tripping over a trailing vacuum cable.
  • Damage to a valuable ornament while dusting.

Without insurance, you are personally responsible for these costs. A single claim for a ruined designer sofa or an injury could cost thousands of pounds, paid directly from your own pocket.

What should a cleaner's policy include?

Not every public liability policy is written with cleaners in mind. When you compare cover, check whether it includes:

  • Damage to property worked upon, sometimes called treatment risks, which covers the item you are actually cleaning. See our guide to treatment risk insurance.
  • Loss of keys, if you hold keys for clients. Our loss of keys cover page explains how it works.
  • A limit of indemnity that matches what your clients ask for, commonly £1 million to £5 million.

What does it cost?

The price depends on your type of cleaning, turnover, staff, the limit you choose and your claims history. For many small cleaning businesses it is a modest annual cost compared with the potential size of a claim.

If you would like cover that fits the way your business works, request a public liability quote and we will send you a short questionnaire to complete online.

faqs.q: Is public liability insurance a legal requirement for cleaners?
faqs.a: No. Public liability insurance is not a legal requirement in the UK, but many clients will not use a cleaner without it.

faqs.q: When does insurance become compulsory for a cleaning business?
faqs.a: Employers' liability insurance is compulsory for most businesses once they employ staff, including part-time and casual workers, with a minimum limit of £5 million.

title: Legal Liability for Cleaners Entering Client Premises
excerpt: Your duty of care, keyholding risks and legal responsibilities when working in a client's home or office.
metaTitle: Legal Liability for Cleaners: Duty of Care Explained
metaDescription: The legal responsibilities of cleaners working in homes and offices: duty of care, negligence, property damage, keyholding and the insurance that protects you.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Insurance documents and a laptop on a desk
content:
When you step into a client's property, whether it is a private home or a commercial office, you take on a significant level of responsibility. It is not just about doing a good job; it is about understanding the legal implications of being on their premises.

Your duty of care

Under UK law, cleaners owe a duty of care to their clients. You must take reasonable steps to make sure your work does not cause harm to the client, their property, or anyone else on the premises, such as visitors or employees.

If you fail in that duty, for example by leaving a wet floor unmarked so that someone slips, or by using the wrong chemical and damaging a worktop, you can be found negligent. Negligence is a failure to take reasonable care that results in damage or injury.

Property damage risks

Accidents happen, even to careful professionals. Common liability risks include:

  • Chemical damage: spilling bleach on a carpet or using an abrasive cleaner on a delicate surface.
  • Breakages: knocking over an expensive vase or damaging electronic equipment while dusting.
  • Water damage: a leaking bucket or hose damaging flooring or the ceiling below.

If you are found liable, you may have to put the client back in the financial position they were in before the incident. That can mean paying for professional repairs or full replacement.

The responsibility of keyholding

Holding keys for a client adds another layer of liability. If you lose a key, you may be responsible for more than the cost of cutting a new one:

  • Lock replacement: changing the locks to restore the property's security.
  • Security consequences: if a lost key can be linked to the property, the situation becomes far more serious.

Use a secure system for managing keys, with coded tags that do not identify the address, and check that your insurance includes loss of keys. Our guide to keyholding risks covers this in more detail.

Protecting yourself

The financial consequences of a liability claim can be devastating for a small business or sole trader. Public liability insurance covers compensation and legal costs if you are held responsible for property damage or injury. For cleaners, check that your policy includes:

  • Damage to property worked upon: many standard policies exclude the item you are actually cleaning, such as the carpet itself.
  • Treatment risks: damage caused by cleaning chemicals or processes.
  • Loss of keys: protection if you lose a client's keys.
Being professional is not just about cleaning well; it is about protecting your client's property and your own livelihood.

If you want to check your cover is right for the work you do, get a quote from our cleaning insurance team.

faqs.q: Can a cleaner be sued for damaging a client's property?
faqs.a: Yes. If the damage was caused by your negligence, the client can claim compensation for repair or replacement. Public liability insurance is designed to cover these claims.

faqs.q: Am I liable if someone slips on a floor I have cleaned?
faqs.a: You can be, if you did not take reasonable care, such as using warning signs. Claims like this are one of the most common reasons cleaners need public liability cover.

title: Public Liability vs Employers' Liability: What's the Difference?
excerpt: We break down the key differences between public and employers' liability, and which your cleaning business actually needs.
metaTitle: Public vs Employers' Liability for Cleaners
metaDescription: The difference between public liability and employers' liability insurance, and which cover is legally required for UK cleaning businesses.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Illustration comparing public liability and employers' liability
content:
Insurance terminology can be confusing, especially when you are trying to get a cleaning business off the ground. Two terms you will hear constantly are public liability and employers' liability. They sound similar, but they cover completely different risks.

Public liability (PL)

Who it protects: your clients and members of the public.

What it covers: claims if someone other than you or your staff is injured, or their property is damaged, because of your business activities.

  • A client trips over a trailing vacuum cord and breaks their arm: public liability covers their compensation claim.
  • You knock over an expensive sculpture while dusting: public liability covers the cost of replacing it.

Is it compulsory? Not legally, but it is practically essential. Many commercial clients will not work with you without it. Read more about public liability insurance for cleaners.

Employers' liability (EL)

Who it protects: your staff, including employees, temporary workers and, often, labour-only subcontractors.

What it covers: claims if an employee is injured or becomes ill because of their work for you.

  • An employee develops a respiratory problem from working with harsh chemicals without proper PPE, or injures their back lifting heavy equipment: employers' liability covers their compensation claim.

Is it compulsory? Yes, for most businesses. Under the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969, if you employ anyone, even on a casual basis, you usually need at least £5 million of cover. The HSE can fine businesses up to £2,500 for every day they are not properly insured. There are limited exemptions, for example some family businesses. See our employers' liability page for details.

Summary

Insurance typeProtectsLegal requirement?
Public liabilityClients and the publicNo, but strongly recommended
Employers' liabilityYour staffYes, for most businesses with employees

If you are growing your team, make sure your cover includes both. Request a quote for public and employers' liability and we will send you a short questionnaire about your business.

faqs.q: Do I need employers' liability insurance if I only employ one person?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Employers' liability is compulsory once you employ anyone, including part-time or casual staff, unless an exemption applies.

faqs.q: Does public liability insurance cover my employees?
faqs.a: No. Injuries to your own employees are covered by employers' liability insurance, not public liability.

title: COSHH Explained Simply: A Cleaner's Guide to Safety
excerpt: Chemical safety does not have to be complicated. Our simple guide to COSHH helps you stay safe and compliant.
metaTitle: COSHH for Cleaners: Chemical Safety Explained
metaDescription: A simple guide to COSHH for UK cleaners: what counts as a hazardous substance, a five-step safety plan, and why it matters for your insurance.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Cleaning chemicals, gloves and safety glasses on a worktop
content:
COSHH stands for the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations. It might sound like dull regulation, but for cleaners it is the law that helps keep you and your staff safe from the chemicals you use every day.

What counts as a hazardous substance?

In cleaning, this usually includes:

  • Bleach and toilet cleaners, which can be corrosive.
  • Oven cleaners, which are often highly caustic.
  • Solvents and descalers.
  • Dust, if your work generates a lot of it.

Your five-step safety plan

You do not need a chemistry degree to work safely. Follow these rules and check the HSE's COSHH guidance for the detail:

  1. Read the label. Never use a product without a label, and look for hazard pictograms. Treat anything marked corrosive with extreme care.
  2. Do not mix chemicals. Mixing bleach with other cleaners, especially acidic limescale removers, can release toxic chlorine gas.
  3. Wear your PPE. Gloves are a barrier between your skin and chemical burns. Use eye protection with sprays that could mist back into your face.
  4. Ventilate. Open a window. Fumes can build up quickly in small bathrooms and cause dizziness.
  5. Know the first aid. Check the safety data sheet for each product so you know what to do if something is swallowed or splashed in the eyes.

Why it matters

Ignoring COSHH can lead to dermatitis, breathing problems or eye injuries. If you employ staff, you are responsible for assessing the risks, providing training and supplying PPE. Good COSHH records also help if a claim is ever made against you.

Chemical damage is also a common source of claims from clients, so check your cleaning business insurance covers treatment risks and damage caused by the products you use. Our guide to treatment risks explains why. When you are ready, get a cleaning insurance quote.

faqs.q: Do self-employed cleaners need to follow COSHH?
faqs.a: COSHH duties apply to employers, and self-employed people have duties to protect themselves and others affected by their work. Following COSHH good practice is sensible for everyone who uses cleaning chemicals.

faqs.q: What is a COSHH assessment?
faqs.a: It is a review of the hazardous substances you use, the risks they pose and the controls you put in place, such as ventilation, PPE and training.

title: The True Cost of a Claim: It's More Than Just the Breakage
excerpt: Think a broken vase just costs the price of a replacement? We explore the hidden costs of liability claims.
metaTitle: The True Cost of a Cleaning Liability Claim
metaDescription: The true cost of a cleaning claim is often far higher than the broken item: compensation, lost earnings, legal costs and the knock-on effects of damage.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: A broken vase on an office floor beside a caution sign
content:
Accidents are an unavoidable part of working in the cleaning industry. But many cleaners underestimate the true financial impact of a small accident.

It is easy to think you will just pay for anything small you break. The direct cost of the item, though, is often just the tip of the iceberg.

Example: the small trip

Imagine you are vacuuming an office reception. You turn around to grab a duster and leave the cord trailing for a few seconds. A visitor walks in, trips and fractures their wrist.

The costs can start to mount quickly:

  • Compensation for the injury, depending on its severity and recovery time.
  • Loss of earnings if the visitor cannot work while they recover.
  • The claimant's legal costs, if the claim succeeds.
  • Your own legal costs to defend the claim.

Once legal costs are added, even a relatively minor injury claim can reach many thousands of pounds. Without public liability insurance, that money comes from your business or personal savings.

The hidden costs of property damage

Simple property damage can spiral too. Suppose you use the wrong product on a limestone floor:

  • Restoration specialists may be needed, and stone restoration is skilled, expensive work.
  • Business interruption: if the floor is in a shop or restaurant that has to close for repairs, the owner may claim for lost income.
  • Reputation damage: hard to put a figure on, but a client who has a bad experience will tell others.

Damage to the floor you were actually treating may not be covered by a basic policy, which is why cleaners should understand damage to property worked upon.

The value of cover

Insurance is a financial safety net and a professional credential. It shows clients you take your business, and their property, seriously. When a claim happens, your insurer handles the investigation, negotiation and settlement, so you can keep running your business.

Want to make sure you are properly protected? Request a public liability quote or read about contract cleaners insurance if you work on commercial sites.

faqs.q: What costs does public liability insurance pay in a claim?
faqs.a: Typically compensation to the third party and legal costs, up to your limit of indemnity and subject to the policy terms and excess.

faqs.q: Should I pay for small breakages myself?
faqs.a: Sometimes that is sensible, depending on your excess, but always tell your insurer or broker about incidents that could lead to a claim, as policies require prompt notification.

title: Keyholding Risks Explained: Protecting Your Client's Security
excerpt: Holding keys for clients is a big responsibility. Learn how to manage keys securely and check your insurance covers you if you lose them.
metaTitle: Keyholding Risks and Insurance for Cleaners
metaDescription: Keyholding risks for cleaners: how to manage client keys securely, what losing a key can really cost, and how loss of keys insurance protects your business.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: House keys on a table next to an insurance policy
content:
For many domestic and commercial cleaners, holding keys is part of the job. It lets you clean while the client is out, which suits everyone. But it also places a real security responsibility on your shoulders.

The real cost of a lost key

If you lose a key, the cost is rarely just a replacement cut. The bigger issue is that the security of the property may now be compromised.

Many clients, and their own insurers, will insist that locks are changed if a key is lost and could be linked to the property. For a commercial building with a master key or electronic access system, that can be very expensive.

Golden rules for key security

  • Never label keys with addresses. A lost key with an address tag is an open invitation. Use a colour or number code instead.
  • Keep a key log. Record who has which key, and when it was signed out and returned.
  • Store keys securely. When not in use, keep them in a locked cabinet or key safe, never on a car dashboard.

Does your insurance cover it?

Standard public liability policies often exclude loss of keys, or limit the cover significantly. Some pay for the key but not the lock replacement.

Loss of keys cover can pay for replacement keys, replacement locks and, depending on the policy, costs such as resetting alarm or access systems. Check the limit is high enough for the most expensive site you hold keys for. See your legal responsibilities on client premises for the wider picture.

Do not risk your reputation on a lost key. Get a quote that includes loss of keys cover.

faqs.q: Is loss of keys included in public liability insurance?
faqs.a: Not always. It is often an extension with its own limit, so check your policy schedule.

faqs.q: What should I do if I lose a client's key?
faqs.a: Tell the client straight away, notify your insurer or broker, and help arrange for locks to be changed if the key could be linked to the property.

title: Handling Accidental Damage: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Breaking a client's item is every cleaner's nightmare. Here is the professional way to handle it.
metaTitle: Handling Accidental Damage as a Cleaner: Step-by-Step
metaDescription: A step-by-step guide for cleaners on handling accidental damage professionally: assessing, documenting, telling the client and contacting your insurer.
keywords: how to tell client about damage
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: A bright, tidy kitchen and living area
content:
It is the sound every cleaner dreads: the crunch of a vacuum against a skirting board, the smash of a vase slipping from a duster, or the snap of a blind mechanism. Accidental damage is, unfortunately, a matter of when rather than if.

How you handle the moments afterwards shows your professionalism and can save the client relationship. Here is what to do when something breaks.

Step 1: stop and assess

Stop what you are doing and make the area safe, for example by carefully picking up broken glass. Do not rush to finish the room.

Step 2: do not attempt a DIY repair

It is tempting to reach for the superglue or scrub harder at a stain. Resist it. Amateur repairs often make the damage worse and can make a professional restoration harder. If you try to hide or fix the damage and fail, you risk losing the client's trust completely.

Step 3: document everything

Before moving anything, if it is safe to do so, take photos:

  • A wide shot showing where the item was.
  • Close-ups of the damage.
  • Keep any broken pieces until the matter is resolved.

Step 4: be honest and immediate

Contact the client as soon as possible. Tell them face to face if they are home, or call them if not; a phone call is better than a note.

You might say: "I am very sorry, but I have had an accident while dusting and damaged your [item]. I wanted to let you know straight away. I have taken photos and will contact my insurer."

Step 5: contact your insurer or broker

Report the incident promptly, as policies usually require. Your broker can help you understand whether a claim makes sense given your excess. Bear in mind that a standard policy may not cover damage to the item you were cleaning; our guide to treatment risks explains why.

Clients can forgive an accident, but they rarely forgive a cover-up.

If you clean in people's homes, read about domestic cleaners insurance, and request a quote to make sure accidents like these are covered.

faqs.q: Should I tell the client before contacting my insurer?
faqs.a: Tell the client promptly and honestly, then notify your insurer or broker as soon as possible. Avoid admitting legal liability or promising payment until you have spoken to your insurer.

faqs.q: Will my insurance pay for something I broke while cleaning it?
faqs.a: Only if your policy covers damage to property worked upon. Many standard public liability policies exclude it, so check your cover.

title: Treatment Risks: The Gap in Standard Public Liability
excerpt: Most standard public liability policies will not pay for the item you are actually cleaning. We explain damage to property worked upon.
metaTitle: Treatment Risk Insurance Explained for Cleaners
metaDescription: Why many standard public liability policies exclude damage to the item you are cleaning, and how treatment risk and property worked upon cover fill the gap.
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: An upholstered armchair being steam cleaned
content:
Ask most cleaners what their insurance covers and they will say: "If I break something, it pays for it."

That is not always true.

Many standard public liability policies contain an exclusion for damage to property being worked upon. Cover for that gap is often provided by an extension known as treatment risks.

The standard cover

Standard public liability is designed mainly for injury to third parties and accidental damage to surrounding property.

  • Usually covered: you are cleaning a window, step back and knock over a vase on a table behind you. You were not working on the vase.
  • Often excluded: you are cleaning the vase itself and it slips out of your hands. Because you were working on it, a standard policy may exclude the claim.

Why this matters for cleaners

As a cleaner, your whole job is working on property. You scrub floors, wipe worktops, polish mirrors and dust electronics.

If your policy excludes damage to property worked upon, you may have little or no cover for the very task you are paid to do. Scratching a stainless steel hob while scrubbing it, or shrinking a carpet while steam cleaning it, could lead to a declined claim. This is especially important for carpet and upholstery cleaners and oven cleaners.

Check your policy wording

Look through your current insurance documents for exclusions relating to property being worked upon, or for a treatment risks extension. If the exclusion is there and the extension is not, you may be more exposed than you think.

Getting the right cover

A broker who specialises in cleaning insurance will know to ask about treatment risks and can arrange cover that reflects the work you actually do. Do not wait for a claim to be declined: request a quote and tell us what you clean.

faqs.q: What is damage to property worked upon?
faqs.a: It is damage to the specific item or surface you are cleaning or treating at the time, such as the carpet you are shampooing. Many standard liability policies exclude it.

faqs.q: Which cleaners need treatment risk cover?
faqs.a: Any cleaner who works directly on client property benefits from it, and it is particularly important for carpet, upholstery, oven and specialist surface cleaners.

title: Employers' Liability Insurance for Cleaning Companies Explained
excerpt: If your cleaning business has staff, casual helpers or labour-only subcontractors, employers' liability cover is almost certainly a legal requirement. Here is who counts, what the law says, and what insurers will ask you.
metaDescription: Employers' liability insurance is a legal requirement for most UK cleaning companies. Who counts as an employee, £5m minimum cover, fines and certificates.
keywords: do I need employers liability insurance
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: Two cleaning operatives in uniform mopping a corridor floor in an office building with a wet floor sign in place
content:
If your cleaning business employs anyone at all — a full-time supervisor, a weekend window cleaner, your sister who covers the school contract on a Tuesday, or a labour-only subcontractor you pay cash in hand — you almost certainly need employers' liability insurance by law. The Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 requires most employers carrying on business in Great Britain to hold at least £5 million of cover against injury or illness suffered by employees in the course of their work. In practice, most insurers issue policies with a £10 million limit as standard, because many client contracts ask for it.

The part that trips cleaning companies up is not the £5 million figure. It is the definition of "employee". The law looks at the reality of the working relationship, not the label on the invoice. A self-employed cleaner who turns up when you tell them to, wears your polo shirt, uses your machine and your chemicals and cannot send someone else in their place will usually be treated as your employee for insurance purposes, whatever it says on their tax return. Get that judgement wrong and you can be trading uninsured without realising it.

This guide sets out what the law actually requires, who counts, the penalties for getting it wrong, why insurers ask for your employer reference number, and how the certificate rules work. It is general guidance rather than advice about your specific business — if your staffing arrangements are unusual, talk it through with a broker before you decide you are exempt.

Is employers' liability insurance a legal requirement for a cleaning company?

Yes, for the great majority of cleaning businesses with any kind of workforce. The 1969 Act makes it compulsory to insure against liability for bodily injury or disease sustained by your employees arising out of and in the course of their employment in Great Britain. The minimum limit of indemnity — the maximum the insurer will pay for a claim — is £5 million, although you should treat £10 million as the working standard because it is what tenders, facilities management agreements and managing agents routinely specify.

Employers' liability is different from public liability insurance, which covers injury to members of the public and damage to third-party property. Public liability is not compulsory by statute; employers' liability generally is. If you are unclear which does what, our guide on public liability versus employers' liability sets the two side by side.

There are narrow exemptions. The main ones are:

  • A limited company with only one employee, where that employee owns 50% or more of the issued share capital. This is the classic one-person cleaning limited company with a sole director and no staff.
  • Most unincorporated family businesses where every employee is a close relative of the employer — spouse or civil partner, parent, grandparent, step-parent, child, grandchild, stepchild, brother, sister, half-brother or half-sister. This exemption does not apply to limited companies, so a family-run cleaning Ltd employing a spouse still needs cover.
  • Genuinely self-employed people working for themselves with no employees.

Being exempt from the Act is not the same as being safe. If a family member is hurt using your rotary machine, they can still sue, and without a policy you pay the damages and the legal costs personally. Many family cleaning firms buy the cover anyway, and most clients will ask for a certificate regardless of whether you are technically exempt.

Who counts as an employee in a cleaning business?

Insurers and the courts look at the substance of the arrangement. The questions that matter are about control, equipment, materials, payment and substitution. Who decides when and where the work happens? Whose vacuum, ladder and chemicals are used? Are they paid an hourly rate for turning up, or a price for a completed job? Can they send someone else in their place without asking you?

Here is how the common arrangements in cleaning usually fall. Treat it as a guide, not a ruling on your particular set-up.

Who they areTypically need employers' liability?Why
Full-time or part-time PAYE cleanersYesStraightforward employment relationship
Casual, weekend or zero-hours cleanersYesEmployment status does not depend on hours worked
Labour-only subcontractors (you supply kit and chemicals, you direct the work)Yes, in most casesInsurers treat them as employees because you control the work
Bona fide subcontractors (own insurance, own equipment, own methods, priced work)Usually no, but you must verify their own coverThey carry their own liability — evidence it in writing
Agency or temp cleanersCheck the agency contract carefullyResponsibility depends on the terms; do not assume
Work experience students and traineesYesThe Act treats them as employees while on placement
Volunteers and unpaid helpersOften yes — declare themUnpaid does not automatically mean uninsured relationship
Family members in a limited companyYesThe family exemption does not extend to limited companies

The single biggest grey area in our trade is the "self-employed" cleaner who works exclusively for you on your rota. If you would be disappointed rather than indifferent when they sent a stranger to cover their shift, you are probably looking at a labour-only subcontractor. Declare them. The premium difference is far smaller than the cost of an uninsured back injury claim.

What are the penalties for not having employers' liability cover?

The Health and Safety Executive enforces the Act and inspectors can ask to see your certificate at any visit. You can be fined up to £2,500 for each day you are without suitable insurance. You can also be fined up to £1,000 for failing to display the certificate or for refusing to make it available to an inspector who asks.

The fine is rarely the worst of it. The real exposure is the claim itself. Employers' liability claims in cleaning are often not dramatic one-off accidents but slow-burning injuries: a soft tissue back injury from repeatedly lifting a 20kg machine into a van, occupational dermatitis from prolonged contact with degreasers and sanitisers, hand-arm vibration from long shifts on a floor scrubber, or a fractured wrist from a wet stair tread. Damages plus claimant legal costs plus your own defence costs can run well beyond what a small cleaning firm holds in the bank, and a claim can arrive years after the person left your employment. Our guide on the true cost of a claim explains why the headline figure is rarely the whole bill.

Uninsured employers also lose control of the process. With a policy in place, the insurer appoints solicitors, handles correspondence and negotiates. Without one, you are doing all of that yourself while still trying to service contracts.

Your ERN, the certificate and the rules on displaying it

When you apply for cover, the insurer will ask for your employer reference number (ERN), sometimes called your employer PAYE reference. It is the number issued by HMRC when you register as an employer and it appears on P45s, P60s and PAYE correspondence, usually in a format like 123/AB45678.

Insurers are not being nosy. Since 2011, employers' liability insurers have been required to submit policy data, including the ERN, to the Employers' Liability Tracing Office database. That database exists so that a cleaner who develops an industrial disease fifteen years from now can find out who insured their former employer. If you do not have an ERN — for example because every member of staff earns below the PAYE threshold and you are not required to register — say so on the proposal form rather than leaving the field blank.

On certificates, the rules are simpler than many people think:

  • Your insurer must issue a certificate of employers' liability insurance showing the limit of indemnity and the period of cover.
  • You must display it where employees can read it, or make it available to them electronically. An emailed PDF, a copy in the staff handbook or a link on your team app all satisfy the requirement, provided staff know where to find it and can access it reasonably easily.
  • Since 2008 there is no legal obligation to keep certificates for 40 years, but the HSE strongly advises retaining a record of who insured you and when. Disease claims can surface decades later, and a saved PDF costs nothing.

Keep a simple insurance history file: insurer name, policy number, limit and dates for every year you have traded with staff. If you ever face a late-notified claim, that file is what lets your broker find the right insurer.

What employers' liability actually covers for cleaning staff

The policy responds when an employee alleges that their injury or illness was caused by your negligence or breach of statutory duty. It pays compensation awarded to them and the legal costs of defending the claim, up to the limit of indemnity.

Typical cleaning scenarios include:

  • A cleaner slips on a stairwell she has just mopped in an office block and fractures an elbow, alleging no wet floor signs were provided.
  • An operative falls from a step ladder while reaching to clean a high-level light fitting that should have been done from a platform.
  • A team member suffers chemical burns after decanting an acidic washroom cleaner into an unlabelled bottle — a classic COSHH failure.
  • A window cleaner sustains a shoulder injury from repeated pole work, alleging no job rotation or training was provided.
  • A deep cleaning operative develops respiratory symptoms after working in an unventilated plant room.

What it does not cover is equally important. It is not health insurance and it does not pay out simply because someone was hurt at work; there must be legal liability. It does not cover damage to a client's property — that sits with public liability and, for the surfaces and items you are actually working on, with treatment risk cover. It does not cover theft of your machines, which is tools and equipment insurance, nor the cost of replacing a client's locks after a lost fob, which is loss of keys cover.

If you employ staff, you can usually place employers' liability alongside your other covers in one package. Our employers' liability page for cleaning companies sets out how it sits within a wider policy, and you can start a quote through the employers' liability enquiry form in a few minutes.

What insurers ask a cleaning company, and why the answers matter

Under the Insurance Act 2015, commercial customers owe a duty of fair presentation of risk. In plain terms, you must tell the insurer everything a prudent underwriter would want to know, in a clear and accessible way, before the policy starts and at each renewal. Get it wrong and the insurer may be entitled to reduce a claim payment, apply different terms retrospectively or, if the misrepresentation was deliberate or reckless, avoid the policy altogether.

For employers' liability, the questions usually cover:

  • Estimated annual wage roll, split by type of work. Office cleaning, window cleaning at height and industrial deep cleaning are rated differently. Include labour-only subcontractor payments — most insurers ask for these separately.
  • Number of employees, including part-time and casual staff.
  • Height of work. Do your window cleaners use ladders, water-fed poles, cradles or MEWPs? What is the maximum working height? See our window cleaners insurance page for how this is rated.
  • Type of premises worked in — offices and schools sit differently to food production, hospitals or industrial plant.
  • Specialist activities such as biohazard, trauma or void property work, which fall under specialist and deep cleaning insurance.
  • Claims history for the last three to five years, including incidents reported but not yet settled.
  • Health and safety arrangements: risk assessments, COSHH assessments, training records, lone working procedures.

Wage roll estimates are usually adjusted at the end of the policy year. If you win a large contract mid-term and double your headcount, tell your broker at the time rather than waiting for renewal. An honest mid-term adjustment is routine; a surprise at audit is not.

Because our questionnaire at Polished Insurance is built for cleaning businesses, it asks about pole heights, chemical use, key holding and subcontractors rather than generic trade questions that do not apply to you.

Subcontractors, tenders and the paperwork clients ask for

Larger cleaning firms often run a mixed model: employed core staff plus subcontractors for cover and overflow. Two rules keep you out of trouble. First, if a subcontractor works under your direction with your equipment, declare them as labour-only and include their payments in your wage roll. Second, if you use genuine subcontractors with their own businesses, collect and diary their insurance certificates — public liability, and employers' liability if they have staff of their own — and check the renewal dates. A certificate that expired four months ago is worth nothing if their operative is injured on your site.

Contract and commercial tenders almost always specify minimum limits, commonly £10 million employers' liability and £5 million public liability, sometimes more for NHS, education or local authority work. Read the schedule of insurance requirements before you price the job, because upgrading limits mid-tender is easier than explaining a shortfall after award. Our pages on contract cleaners insurance and commercial and office cleaning insurance cover the combinations that tenders typically ask for, and you can request quotes for either through the contract cleaning enquiry form.

Where you hold client keys or alarm codes, expect additional questions about storage and accountability. Our guide to keyholding risks explains what good practice looks like.

A practical checklist for this week

  1. List everyone who does work for your business, including casuals, family members, trainees and subcontractors. Next to each name, note who supplies the equipment and who directs the work.
  2. Decide, honestly, which of them are labour-only. If you are unsure about one, treat them as labour-only and declare them.
  3. Find your ERN on a P60 or PAYE letter and save it somewhere you can reach quickly.
  4. Check your current certificate: is the limit at least £5 million, does the period cover today, and is the insured name exactly the same as your trading entity?
  5. Display the certificate — noticeboard, staff WhatsApp pinned message or handbook — and tell your team where it is.
  6. Collect current insurance certificates from every bona fide subcontractor and put their expiry dates in your calendar.
  7. Check that your written risk assessments are current. If you have five or more employees, the significant findings must be recorded in writing.
  8. Review your COSHH sheets and confirm that every chemical in every van is in a labelled container with the correct dilution instructions.
  9. Confirm your wage roll estimate still matches reality. If you have grown, tell your broker.
  10. Save a copy of every past employers' liability certificate in a dated folder so you can trace old insurers if a late claim appears.

Reducing the chance of a claim in the first place

Insurers price on exposure and on how well you manage it. The controls that matter most in cleaning are unglamorous and cheap: wet floor signs carried in every kit bag and actually used; a rule that nobody works above shoulder height from a stool or chair; correct ladder training or, better, water-fed poles for anything routine; trolleys and lifting aids so operatives are not carrying machines down stairs; gloves and eye protection stored with the chemicals rather than in the van; and a lone working check-in for evening cleans in empty buildings.

Record the training. A signed induction sheet showing that an operative was shown how to dilute a product and where the safety data sheets are kept is one of the most useful documents you can produce when a claim lands two years later. The same discipline helps with client-side incidents too — our guide on handling accidental damage walks through what to record at the time and why it matters. If you are still weighing up which covers your business genuinely needs, start with do I really need insurance for my cleaning business, or browse all our cleaning insurance guides.

Getting employers' liability cover in place

If you have taken on your first member of staff, or you have realised that the "self-employed" cleaner on your rota is really a labour-only subcontractor, put cover in place before the next shift rather than at the next renewal. Cover is subject to the policy wording, the insurer's acceptance and your circumstances, so the sensible step is a short conversation rather than a guess.

You can tell us about your team, your wage roll and the type of work you do through the employers' liability insurance enquiry form, or see the full range of covers on our cleaning insurance hub. If you would rather talk through an unusual staffing arrangement first, use the general enquiry form and we will come back to you.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need employers' liability insurance if I am a sole trader cleaner with no staff?

If you genuinely work alone with no employees, no casual helpers and no labour-only subcontractors, the Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 does not apply to you. You would still normally want public liability cover, and if you occasionally bring in a friend or family member to help on a big job, you need to declare that. Even one paid helper for a single end of tenancy clean can create an employment relationship — see our end of tenancy cleaning insurance page for how these jobs are typically rated.

How much employers' liability cover does a cleaning company legally need?

The legal minimum is £5 million. Most insurers issue employers' liability at £10 million as standard because that is what commercial contracts, managing agents and public sector tenders commonly specify. Check the insurance schedule of any tender before you price the work.

Does employers' liability insurance cover my subcontractors?

It depends on the type of subcontractor and how they are declared. Labour-only subcontractors — those who work under your direction using your equipment and materials — are usually treated as employees and should be included in your declared wage roll. Bona fide subcontractors who run their own businesses, price their own work and carry their own insurance are normally outside your policy, but you should obtain and diary copies of their certificates.

What happens if I do not have employers' liability insurance?

The HSE can fine you up to £2,500 for each day you trade without suitable cover, and up to £1,000 for failing to display the certificate or to show it to an inspector on request. More significantly, you would be personally liable for any compensation and legal costs if an employee brings a successful injury claim against you.

Why does my insurer need my employer reference number?

Employers' liability insurers must submit policy details, including the ERN, to the Employers' Liability Tracing Office database so that former employees can identify the correct insurer if they bring a claim years later. Your ERN appears on P60s, P45s and PAYE correspondence from HMRC. If you are not registered for PAYE because all staff earn below the threshold, tell your broker rather than leaving the question unanswered.

Do I still have to display the certificate on a wall?

No. You must make the certificate available to employees, and electronic display is acceptable — an email, a shared drive, a staff app or a copy in the handbook — provided your team know where it is and can access it without difficulty. For a mobile cleaning workforce, electronic access is usually the more practical option.

title: Public Liability Limits for Cleaning Contracts Explained
excerpt: Cleaning contracts usually specify £1m, £2m, £5m or £10m of public liability cover. Here is how buyers decide, what limit suits your work, and what to do when a tender asks for more than you hold.
metaTitle: Public Liability Limit for Cleaning Contracts
metaDescription: How much public liability cover does a cleaning contract need? Compare £1m, £2m, £5m and £10m limits, how buyers set them and what to do if a tender asks more.
keywords: how much public liability insurance for cleaners
author: Polished Insurance team
heroAlt: A cleaner in uniform mopping the floor of a large office reception area with a wet floor sign nearby
content:
Most UK cleaning contracts specify a public liability limit of between £1 million and £5 million. Small domestic and sole-trader work is usually happy with £1m or £2m. Once you move into offices, schools, retail units, managing agents and facilities work, £5 million becomes the everyday expectation. £10 million is asked for by a narrower group of buyers: NHS trusts, airports and rail, large housing associations, universities, some local authorities and national facilities management firms who pass their own client requirements down the chain.

The limit in a contract is not a measure of how careful you are. It is the buyer's way of making sure that if something goes badly wrong on their site, there is enough money behind your business to deal with it without them being dragged into it. That is why the number is often set by a procurement template rather than by anyone who has looked at what cleaning actually involves — and why a two-person office cleaning firm can find itself asked for the same £10m limit as a groundworks contractor.

This guide explains what a limit really covers, how the common limits compare, what different types of cleaning work tend to need, and the practical steps to take when a tender asks for more cover than you currently hold. If you want the cover detail alongside it, our contract cleaners insurance page sets out how these policies are usually built.

What does a public liability limit of indemnity actually mean?

The limit of indemnity is the most your insurer will pay for a single claim made against you by a third party — a client, a member of the public, a tenant, a passer-by — for injury or property damage you are legally liable for. It normally includes the legal costs of defending the claim, and those costs alone can be substantial even when a claim is eventually dropped.

Two details matter more than most people realise:

  • "Any one claim" versus "in the aggregate". Public liability is usually written on an "any one claim" or "any one occurrence" basis, meaning the full limit is available for each separate incident during the policy year. Some sections — pollution or products, for example — may be capped in the aggregate, which means the limit is the total for the whole year however many claims arise. A contract asking for "£5m any one occurrence" will not be satisfied by £5m in the aggregate.
  • Sub-limits inside the policy. The headline number rarely applies to everything. Damage to property worked upon (harm to the actual item or surface you were cleaning, such as a carpet that shrinks or a stone floor that etches) is often subject to a much lower inner limit, and in some wordings is excluded altogether. The same goes for loss of keys, damage to underground services, and damage caused by heat or water application. We cover this gap in detail in our guide to treatment risks and standard public liability.

There is also the excess: the first part of each claim you pay yourself. A £5m limit with a high property damage excess can be less useful day to day than a £2m limit with a modest excess, because most cleaning claims are small breakages and marks, not catastrophes. If you have not seen how the smaller claims add up, our guide on the true cost of a cleaning claim is worth ten minutes.

£1m, £2m, £5m or £10m: how the common limits compare

LimitTypically required byWhat to know
£1 millionPrivate householders, some small letting agents, market stall and low-risk one-off workThe old default. Increasingly refused by commercial buyers, and often only marginally cheaper than £2m.
£2 millionSmall offices, shops, cafés, estate and letting agents, many franchise agreementsA sensible working minimum for any business entering client premises regularly.
£5 millionManaging agents, schools and academies, care homes, larger commercial landlords, most public sector frameworksThe most commonly specified figure in UK cleaning contracts. Usually the practical benchmark if you tender at all.
£10 millionNHS trusts, rail and aviation, universities, large housing providers, national FM companies, some councilsOften a flow-down requirement from the buyer's own contracts. Available from many insurers, sometimes by adding an excess layer on top of a £5m primary policy.

A point worth making to nervous clients: moving from £2m to £5m does not usually double your premium. Insurers price mainly on your activities, turnover, wage roll and claims history — what you do and how much of it. The limit is a factor, but a smaller one than most buyers assume. If a contract worth real money hinges on the limit, it is nearly always worth asking us to quote both.

How do contract buyers decide what limit to ask for?

In practice, four things drive the number:

  • The buyer's own contracts. A facilities management company cleaning a bank's head office will be required to hold, say, £10m, and will push the same requirement onto every subcontractor so there is no weak link. This is the single most common reason a small firm gets asked for a figure that looks disproportionate.
  • The value and visibility of the site. A glass-fronted atrium, a listed building, a data centre, a hospital ward or a school full of children all raise the potential consequences of a mistake. Higher footfall means a greater chance that a wet floor injures someone who is not an employee.
  • Procurement templates and insurers' advice. Many public bodies use a standard schedule of insurance requirements across all suppliers, from window cleaners to construction. Nobody sat down and decided cleaners specifically need £10m.
  • Worst-case injury cost. Serious injury claims involving long-term care and loss of earnings can run into seven figures once damages, care costs and legal fees are added together. A buyer setting a £5m or £10m limit is thinking about that scenario, not about a scratched desk.

Could a cleaning claim really reach millions?

Most cleaning claims are modest. The ones that are not tend to share a pattern: the cleaning itself was routine, but the consequences spread.

  • A visitor slips on a freshly mopped hard floor in a busy reception, hits their head, and is left unable to return to work. Damages for care, adaptations and lost earnings over decades sit in a different bracket to a broken lamp.
  • A tap or hose left running overnight in a fourth-floor kitchenette floods three floors of a let office building. The claim is not just the carpets — it is IT equipment, drying and reinstatement, and the tenants' loss of use of the space.
  • A pressure washer used near a client's electrical intake or a window cleaner's pole contacting an overhead line escalates instantly from property damage to serious injury.
  • A cleaning chemical decanted into an unlabelled bottle is used by a client's staff member, causing burns and a regulatory investigation. Our plain-English guide to COSHH covers the controls that stop this happening.

The point is not to frighten anyone. It is that the limit exists for the tail end of the distribution, and that tail is what a buyer is buying protection from.

What limit does your type of cleaning usually need?

Every contract differs, but these are the patterns we see across cleaning businesses:

  • Domestic cleaning and housekeeping: £1m to £2m satisfies almost all private clients, though agencies and introducer platforms often set £2m as their floor. See domestic cleaners insurance for what else these policies typically include.
  • Office and commercial cleaning: £2m for small independent premises, £5m once managing agents, landlords or national tenants are involved. Our commercial and office cleaning insurance page explains the usual structure.
  • Contract cleaning with employees across multiple sites: £5m as standard, with £10m needed for some frameworks. Employers' liability sits alongside it.
  • Window cleaning: £1m to £2m for domestic rounds, £5m for commercial blocks and anything at height. If you work above ground floor level, check the height and access conditions on your window cleaners insurance.
  • Carpet, upholstery and hard floor cleaning: the limit matters less than the treatment risk and property worked upon cover on your carpet and upholstery cleaners insurance, because the likely claim is the item itself.
  • End of tenancy work: £2m is common, with agents increasingly asking for £5m plus loss of keys cover.
  • Pressure washing and exterior cleaning: £5m is often required on commercial forecourts and car parks, partly because of overspray, run-off and surface damage exposures.
  • Specialist and deep cleaning (biohazard, post-incident, kitchen ducting): usually £5m upwards, and the activity description matters as much as the number.

What to do when a tender asks for more cover than you hold

Do not withdraw and do not tick the box hoping nobody checks. Buyers verify certificates, and a false declaration in a tender is a contractual problem as well as an insurance one. Work through this instead:

  1. Read the exact wording. Is it "£5,000,000 public liability" or "£5,000,000 any one occurrence, unlimited in the period"? Does it also demand employers' liability of £10m, professional indemnity, or cover for damage to property in your care, custody and control? Copy the clause out in full before you ask anyone to price it.
  2. Check whether the requirement is conditional on award. Many tenders accept a broker letter confirming that the required limits can be put in place if the contract is won. That is normal and we provide it regularly.
  3. Ask us to quote the higher limit. Increasing from £2m to £5m, or £5m to £10m, is often straightforward once the insurer understands the work. Send the tender clause with your contract cleaners insurance enquiry so it is priced against the actual requirement rather than a guess.
  4. Look at the additional clauses, not just the number. Tenders commonly require indemnity to principal (extending your cover to the client in respect of your work), a waiver of subrogation (your insurer giving up the right to recover from the client), a cross liability clause, or 30 days' notice of cancellation. These have to be checked against the policy wording, and some are simply not available from every insurer.
  5. Negotiate if the limit is disproportionate. If you clean a village hall twice a week and the council template demands £10m, it is reasonable to ask whether £5m is acceptable for this scope. Buyers do sometimes flex. Put the request in writing early, not after award.
  6. Get the certificate right. The legal entity name on the certificate must match the name on the tender, and the described business activities must cover everything you will do on site. A certificate that says "office cleaning" will be queried if the contract includes external window cleaning and jet washing.

The other covers a cleaning contract usually asks for

Public liability is rarely the only line in the insurance clause. Expect some combination of:

  • Employers' liability if you have any staff. The Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance) Act 1969 requires a minimum of £5 million, most policies are issued at £10 million, and the HSE can fine up to £2,500 for each day you trade without valid cover. Our guide to employers' liability for cleaning companies covers who counts as an employee, including casual and zero-hours staff. If the difference between the two liability covers is still fuzzy, read public liability versus employers' liability.
  • Loss of keys and keyholding cover where you hold access devices. Replacing a suited master key system or reprogramming fobs across a block is expensive, and standard property damage wording may not reach it. See loss of keys insurance and our keyholding risks guide.
  • Professional indemnity where you advise on specifications, TUPE, cleaning regimes or infection control, or where a facilities contract includes a service level guarantee. Details on professional indemnity for cleaning and facilities companies. Watch the retroactive date — the earliest date of work the policy will respond to — because a new policy may not cover advice you gave two years ago.
  • Tools, equipment and stock, sometimes required so the buyer is not left without machinery mid-contract. See tools and equipment insurance for cleaners.

Checklist before you sign a cleaning contract

  • Copy the full insurance clause into a document and tick each requirement off against your schedule, not your certificate summary.
  • Confirm the basis of the limit: any one claim or occurrence, versus in the aggregate.
  • Check the property worked upon and treatment risk sub-limits against the value of what you handle.
  • Check the care, custody and control position for client property you move, store or hold keys to.
  • Confirm the excess for property damage and make sure you could fund it on every site you run.
  • Make sure every activity in the specification appears in your policy's business description, including any at height, external, pressure washing or specialist work.
  • Identify whether you use labour-only subcontractors — workers you supply and supervise who do not bring their own materials or tools — and confirm they are treated as employees under the policy rather than left uncovered.
  • Ask whether indemnity to principal, waiver of subrogation and cancellation notice periods can be granted in writing.
  • Diarise your renewal date against the contract term so cover never lapses mid-contract, and send the new certificate to the client automatically.
  • Tell your broker about any change in activities, sites, turnover or staff numbers during the year. Under the duty of fair presentation in the Insurance Act 2015, commercial customers must disclose everything a prudent insurer would want to know; getting this wrong can reduce or void a claim.

Choosing your limit when no contract specifies one

If you work mainly for private clients, nobody is going to hand you a number. Set it by asking what the worst realistic incident on your rounds looks like. A domestic cleaner working alone in modest houses is in a different position to a team cleaning a busy dental practice, a nursery or a hotel kitchen. Consider the number of people around while you work, the value of the building and its contents, whether you use water or heat, and whether you work at height.

In our experience £2m is the sensible floor for anyone entering client premises for money, and £5m is the pragmatic choice for any business that wants to bid for commercial work without re-papering its insurance every time a tender lands. You can compare the full range of covers on our cleaning insurance hub, or browse the rest of our cleaning business guides for the practical side of claims and site risk, including what to do in the first hour after accidental damage.

Getting the right limit in place

Limits are easy to change and awkward to get wrong halfway through a contract. If you have a tender on your desk with an insurance schedule you are not sure about, send it over with your details and we will tell you plainly whether your current cover meets it and what the higher limit would look like. Our questionnaire only asks the questions that apply to cleaning businesses, so you are not answering irrelevant trade questions to get a sensible answer.

Start with a contract cleaners insurance quote, or use the general enquiry form if your work spans several types of cleaning. This guide is general information rather than personal advice — cover always depends on the policy wording, the insurer's acceptance and your own circumstances, so talk it through with a broker before you commit to a contract.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is £1 million public liability enough for a cleaning business?

It can be enough for straightforward domestic work for private householders, but it is increasingly below what commercial clients accept. Many managing agents, schools and public sector buyers specify £5 million as a minimum, and the price difference between £1m and £2m is usually small. If you have any ambition to take on commercial contracts, £2m or £5m is the more practical starting point.

Why do cleaning tenders ask for £10 million public liability?

Usually because the buyer is required to hold that limit under its own contracts and passes the same requirement down to every supplier, regardless of trade. It is a procurement template decision rather than a judgement about cleaning risk. Many insurers will write £10m for cleaning businesses, sometimes by adding an excess layer above a £5m primary policy. It is also worth asking the buyer whether £5m is acceptable for a limited scope.

Does a higher public liability limit cost a lot more?

Premium is driven mainly by your activities, turnover, wage roll, claims history and the sites you work on, with the limit as a smaller factor. Increasing from £2m to £5m rarely doubles the cost. Any figures quoted are illustrative only and depend entirely on your circumstances and the insurer's assessment, so the only reliable answer is a quotation against the specific limit you need.

Does my public liability limit cover damage to the thing I was cleaning?

Not always, and often not up to the full limit. Damage to the item or surface you were working on is treated separately in many policies, either through a lower inner limit for damage to property worked upon or a treatment risk extension. This matters most for carpet, upholstery, stone floor, oven and pressure washing work, where the likely claim is the item itself rather than an injury.

What is indemnity to principal and will my policy provide it?

It extends your public liability cover to your client in respect of liability arising from the work you do for them, so the client is protected under your policy for your activities. Cleaning contracts and facilities management agreements request it regularly. Availability depends on the insurer and wording, so ask before you sign rather than assuming it is included.

Do I need to tell my insurer when I win a new contract?

Yes, if it changes anything material: new types of work, working at height, new sites, higher turnover, extra staff or subcontractors, or a contract that imposes clauses your policy does not currently meet. Commercial customers have a duty of fair presentation under the Insurance Act 2015, and failing to disclose a material change can affect how a claim is settled.
